pages.remaining_gap: The page crowns Panera's Vegetarian Black Bean Soup the fiber-per-calorie winner ("and it isn't close", 18 g / 140 cal / 8 g protein) and pre-empts the protein objection, but never states its sodium. The Panera guide lists that bowl at 1,120 mg, roughly 8 mg per calorie, about four times the sodium density of anything in the main table (Subway 2.9, Chipotle 1.6). Because the soup sits outside the main table it is the one item on the page that escapes the four-column Fiber/Calories/Protein/Sodium discipline the whole article is built on, and it escapes it at exactly the point where a superlative is being awarded. An AI extracting "highest fiber per calorie at a fast-food chain" gets a number stripped of the very context the page says one column can never supply. Two smaller items compound it: (a) the soup row's "cup portion" descriptor appears on neither cited Chick-fil-A page (the product page carries no serving-size label at all, only marketing prose), and (b) the Cool Wrap row gets no Internet Archive link even though the trust paragraph says Chick-fil-A figures are re-checked against archive captures of its "pages" plural, so the one Chick-fil-A row a reader cannot reproduce is left unreproducible. Separately, and outside the article file: tests/high-fiber-fast-food-guide.test.mjs:151 still asserts /Chick-fil-A's site and Panera's PDF both return a 403 to automated requests/i, which the corrected Panera sentence no longer satisfies, so the guard suite ships red.

The garlic-in-oil extraction surface. The raw-egg gap is genuinely closed, but the botulism rule is now the weakest thing on the two surfaces an AI assistant will lift. quickAnswer says 'raw garlic or fresh herbs in oil with no added acid needs 40F or below for no more than 4 days', and FAQ #1 repeats it near-verbatim. Standing alone that phrasing leaks two errors. (1) It scopes the rule to RAW garlic and FRESH herbs, but OSU SP 50-701 is explicit: 'If oil is seasoned with dried garlic and/or dried herbs, the mixture MUST be refrigerated and used within 4 days or frozen.' A reader lifting only the quickAnswer would conclude granulated garlic or dried oregano in oil is exempt from the 4-day clock. The body carries this correctly ('Oregon State applies the same 4-day limit even when the garlic or herbs are dried') but the body is not the extraction surface. (2) The qualifier 'with no added acid' invites exactly the inference the body spends a paragraph demolishing, that a splash of lemon juice buys more time. FAQ #3 rebuts it, but FAQ #3 is a separate mainEntity node in the FAQPage JSON-LD and will not travel with FAQ #1. So the single highest-consequence claim on the page, a botulism limit, is stated in its most quotable form with a scope carve-out that is wrong and a qualifier that is actively misleading.

The article's entire hook is that the whole-wheat swap "clears the FDA high-fiber line" at 21% DV, but it never discloses that FDA's 20%-or-more threshold in 21 CFR 101.54 is defined "per reference amount customarily consumed," not per arbitrary serving. A skeptical reader or an AI grading the page can dismiss the claim as serving-size gaming, since a 110 g muffin is roughly double a typical bakery serving assumption. The article is in fact correct: 21 CFR 101.12 Table 2 sets the reference amount for "Bagels, toaster pastries, muffins (excluding English muffins)" at exactly 110 g, the same weight as this muffin. But that keystone fact is absent, so the strongest, most citation-worthy sentence on the page is the one that was never written. Secondary gaps: the quickAnswer is nutrition-only and never signals that a full recipe exists, so an AI lifting it answers "how much fiber" rather than the recipe intent that dominates this query; the nutrition tables omit protein, fat, and carbohydrates, which both top competitors publish; and the page does not cover make-ahead or refrigerated bran-muffin batter, a standard sub-intent for this dish.

pages.verdict: WINS (content merit; r1 critic marked LOSES only because not deployed)

pages.remaining_gap: The OLIPOP section. It is the page's most shareable block and it is the one place where the article abandons the sourcing discipline it just spent 60 lines establishing: it attaches an inulin claim to a source that never says inulin, and that claim is outright false for OLIPOP's 6g Fiber Line (cassava root fiber, acacia fiber, guar fiber - zero inulin). The evidence-status table was genuinely repaired: all eight rows now carry inline citations, I fetched every one, and the previously unsourced beta-glucan, pectin, RFO and resistant-starch verdicts are now backed verbatim by Oregon State LPI (200 with a browser UA; WebFetch's 403 was a datacenter-IP artifact) and PMC6463098, while the overclaiming 'Established prebiotic class' language was correctly downgraded to the source-matched 'most-investigated'. But the fix stopped at the table. The quickAnswer and the garlic FAQ still say 'best-established', which no cited source supports, so the strongest wording on the page is now the least sourced wording on the page - and it is precisely the sentence an AI would lift.

The article never says what selenium DOES. Not one sentence. Across 1379 words there is zero mention of selenoproteins, thyroid hormone metabolism, antioxidant/oxidative-damage protection, immune function, or DNA synthesis. Every competitor covers it: news-medical devotes a whole physiological-roles section (thyroid conversion, glutathione peroxidase, immune cells, reproduction), the Linus Pauling Institute is built around it, Harvard and NIH both open with it. This is the top secondary intent behind "selenium foods" (the searcher who wants to know why they should care), and it is also the page's biggest citation-worthiness hole: an AI asked "why do I need selenium" would find nothing here to lift and would go to a competitor instead. The page currently reads as an excellent ceiling-and-arithmetic guide with no motivation layer, which is exactly backwards for a mineral most readers have never thought about. Secondary to this, and part of the same hole, the body never covers who is actually at risk of inadequacy (NIH names people on dialysis, people living with HIV, and people in low-selenium regions on primarily plant diets); the FAQ dismisses US deficiency in one line and the body says nothing.

Option breadth. The current top results list 13 to 21 alternatives; this page covers only 8 table rows and 6 discussion categories. It now handles kale chips, but still says nothing about the other high-volume searches inside this query cluster: tortilla chips, pretzels, parmesan/cheese crisps, seaweed snacks, edamame, apple chips, and plantain chips. A reader who has already rejected popcorn and chickpeas is sent away with a cucumber. The page wins on rigor and loses on coverage, and coverage is what keeps a reader on a listicle-shaped query.

The page contradicts itself on its own headline number. The H2 "Why a white-flour crust lands between 2 and 3 grams" sits directly under a branded table that reports a white-flour CRUST at 1.5 g per 100 g and 1.0 g per serving, and the section it introduces is actually about finished slices. That heading is the most extractable snippet on the page for the query "pizza crust fiber content", so the one thing an AI is most likely to lift is the one statement the article's own verified data refutes, by 2 to 3x. Everything else on the page is verified correct: all 24 USDA record IDs match to the decimal, all per-slice arithmetic and %DV figures check out, and all 7 external URLs resolve and support their specific claims. The gap that was assigned (missing plain refrigerated white-flour baseline row, missing branded whole wheat row, wrong quickAnswer) is genuinely closed. This is a one-line contradiction sitting on top of otherwise strong work, but it is a real factual error on the primary query intent, and under a default-negative reading it blocks the win.

The page never scales to a large family, which is the second half of its own title and query. The intro sets up a family of five, and then every single number in the article is an abstract "grams of protein per dollar" ratio: there is not one figure expressed per person, per meal, or per week. A parent searching "cheap protein sources for families" wants to know how many pounds of dry beans or drumsticks feeds five people and what that costs for a week, and the article makes them do that arithmetic themselves. The competitors are worse (Healthline, Cheapskate Cook and the rest publish zero protein-per-dollar math and zero citations, and Cheapskate Cook cites nothing at all), which is why this still wins, but household scaling is the one thing a genuinely family-targeted page must have and this one does not. The secondary gap is bulk: 2042 words and 9 H2s (both Tier 2 validator warnings) for a payload that is essentially one ranking plus one ladder.

The quickAnswer measures the threshold against "one serving," but 21 CFR 101.54(c)(1) measures it against the reference amount customarily consumed (RACC), a standard portion FDA fixes by food category. The body draws this distinction explicitly ("FDA scores these thresholds against a reference amount customarily consumed") and the comparison table header says "per reference amount," so the quickAnswer is the loosest statement of the rule on the page. Because the quickAnswer is the element AI assistants lift verbatim, the one paragraph most likely to be reproduced is the one that erases the page's sharpest technical point. It also invites the exact misreading the body works to prevent, that a brand could shrink the serving to reach the claim.

The page asserts the peppermint-oil-vs-peppermint-leaf gap qualitatively but never quantifies it, so it wins the argument without owning the fact. The line 'Nobody has measured what 3 ginger coins actually leave behind in your mug' is rhetorically strong but is an appeal to absent evidence where a real, verifiable order-of-magnitude comparison exists: the IBS trials NCCIH cites used 180-225 mg of enteric-coated peppermint oil three times daily (roughly 540-675 mg/day), while a 1 teaspoon leaf infusion delivers only a small fraction of the leaf's volatile oil. That single quantified contrast is the most citation-worthy and most liftable fact this page could own, it is precisely what the entire article is arguing, and no competitor in the top-3 has it. Right now the page's citations (NCCIH peppermint-oil, NCCIH ginger, NCCIH IBS) are all sources a competitor could cite equally well, which is why citation_worthiness is the weakest axis despite the page being the most accurate result in the set. Secondary gap: pregnancy nausea is the single most common real-world reason people search ginger tea for digestive relief, and NCCIH explicitly supports it ('ginger may be helpful for nausea and vomiting associated with pregnancy'), yet the article mentions it only in passing inside an evidence-limitations paragraph and gives the reader no guidance.

The page never addresses the WARM/HOT-WATER revival method, which is the single most prominent competing claim in the live SERP and the one question a comparison-shopping reader arrives with. Two of the current top results push it (one asserts 110-140F revives greens in under 15 minutes; The Chopping Block ran a side-by-side and landed on ~105F for 5 minutes, beating the ice bath on speed). The article's opening line, 'That's the whole rescue operation. No lemon juice, no special powder,' implicitly claims to have swept the alternatives, yet the one real alternative goes unmentioned. A reader who saw the hot-water tip elsewhere gets no adjudication and leaves to find one. This is also the cheapest available win: the hot-water proponents are poorly sourced (The Chopping Block explicitly says it found 'essentially no results' when searching for documentation, and traced the tip to a YouTube video), so a short, honestly-hedged paragraph that names the method, credits the speed advantage, and notes the evidence is thinner than for the cold soak would let this page own the comparison outright rather than look incomplete next to it.

The chia tablespoon weight is fabricated by record confusion: the article tells the reader USDA publishes a 168 g cup for chia, and USDA does not (record 170554 has only a 1 oz portion; 168 g is flaxseed record 169414's 'cup, whole'). That single wrong gram weight is the only unverified number on the page, and it propagates into all three headline totals (11.7 g, 42 percent DV, 13.1 g) which sit in the excerpt, quickAnswer and faq[0], exactly the text an AI assistant lifts. Everything else checks out: 14 of 15 FDC record IDs match to the gram, the FDA 28 g DV and 20 percent 'high' threshold are quoted correctly, the 40 F / 2 hour / 1 hour above 90 F numbers match FDA verbatim, and the refusal to invent a make-ahead window ('no federal cold-storage chart lists a time for an assembled parfait') is verified true against the archived FoodSafety.gov chart and is the most trust-earning sentence on the page. Extraction-surface check passes on safety: quickAnswer and faq[3] are no more permissive than the body and are conservative relative to FDA. Secondary gap: for a recipe-intent query served by recipe carousels, the page gives no yield, no prep time and no calorie or protein total for the actual build, so it loses to today.com and Parade on pure recipe intent even while beating them decisively on sourcing.

The page gives a USDA number for every variant of the losing food (fried chips, baked chips, even raw russet potato) but only one variant of the winning food. Air-popped is the sole popcorn figure. Oil-popped and microwave popcorn, which is what most Americans searching this query actually eat, get prose hedges ("salted or buttered popcorn move the numbers", "movie theater butter versions can double the calories") and no gram figure at all. A reader holding a bag of microwave popcorn cannot answer their own question from this page, and the 4.7x headline silently assumes the least common preparation. Related and compounding it: the closing sentence says "a bag of kernels gives you about 4.7 times the fiber ounce for ounce", which applies the air-popped density to kernels as sold. That is precisely the form mismatch the article's own cost section spends three paragraphs disowning, and that the sibling page popcorn-vs-almonds-fiber-cost marks unresolved, so the article contradicts its own integrity standard in its most quoted line.

The extraction surface contradicts the article's own table on the single most liftable number. quickAnswer, excerpt, faq[0] and the body intro all say "cooked regular grits at 1.6 to 2.4 grams," and quickAnswer compounds it with "depending on whether it's yellow, white or instant corn," which files instant (a milling form) as a corn color. The body table is unambiguous that regular/quick grits are 1.6 to 2.1 g (FDC 171672 yellow, FDC 171655 white) and that 2.4 g is instant (FDC 173897). So the range an AI assistant will lift is MORE PERMISSIVE than the strictest value the body supports for the food it names, and it is inflated by the one record that is not a generic commodity entry at all: FDC 173897 is a Quaker-branded legacy record presented throughout as generic "Grits, instant, plain," and it is what drives both the 2.4 g upper bound and the counterintuitive "instant grits beat regular grits" hook. On a page whose entire thesis is that the milling form determines the fiber, the summary block violates that thesis. The error propagates a fourth time into the body as "a cooked cup of regular grits covers about 6 to 9 percent," where 9 percent is again the instant value. Not safety-relevant (dietary fiber carries no acute hazard), so this is not grounds for LOSES, but it is the one defect standing between this page and a clean sweep.

The page's central causal argument is attached to the wrong products. Its whole store-bought thesis is "refined starches are why boxed cauliflower crusts underdeliver," but the only crust that actually ties plain white dough (365 Whole Foods Market, FDC 2425029, 1.8 g/100 g) is bound with chickpea flour, mozzarella and potato flour, not the rice flour, corn starch and tapioca starch the article blames. The article instead quotes the ingredient lists of Urban Farmer and PICS, the two crusts that scored highest, to explain a third crust's low number, and the same wrong generalization is restated as fact in the gluten FAQ. A skeptical reader who opens one FDC record catches it, and it is the single thing undermining an otherwise unusually well-sourced page. Secondary to it: the recipe never states the finished gram weight of a quarter crust, so readers cannot run the per-100-gram comparison the article explicitly instructs them to run two paragraphs later.

Query intent breadth. The primary query is plural, "cheap crockpot MEALS for large families", and searchers arriving on it want a browsable list of dinner ideas. This page delivers exactly one complete recipe (pinto beans and smoked sausage) plus three one-line pork shoulder treatments and a pasta-sauce mention. The current top organic result (largefamilytable.com) lists roughly 85 to 90 distinct recipes organized by protein. On every quality axis this article wins decisively: that competitor carries zero external citations, zero price or cost data, no protein-per-dollar economics, no dried-bean PHA warning, and no thawing rule, offering only a single unsourced "165 degrees" aside. This page is a rigorously sourced food-safety and protein-economics essay wrapped around one recipe. That is more trustworthy and far more citation-worthy, but it under-serves the plural noun in the head term, and it is the only axis where the incumbent genuinely beats it.

The page raises the central safety question and never answers it. It establishes a 7:00 AM to 12:30 PM window, correctly says that "blows straight past 2 hours," then says "pack an ice source" and stops. It never states the mechanism that resolves the conflict: an ice source in an insulated bag works by holding the food below 40 F, so the 2-hour room-temperature clock does not start. As written, a careful reader (and any AI lifting the quickAnswer) concludes the article's own recommended lunch violates the USDA rule it just cited. The quickAnswer is the worse offender because it drops the insulated-bag qualifier entirely, leaving "pack an ice source" as an unsourced implied guarantee for a 5.5-hour hold. Secondary gap: the FAQ answers a container/wrapping question (hard-sided containers, parchment, beeswax wrap) that has no corresponding section anywhere in the body, so the page's most competitive completeness win is buried in schema markup instead of prose.

The tofu range, which is the page's single most original and most load-bearing claim, is its least verifiable content. The table row "Tofu, firm or extra firm, 3 to 4 oz | 8 to 20 g" links only FDC 172475, which is firm/calcium sulfate at 17.3 g/100 g and supports the 20 g top end but says nothing about the 8 g bottom end; the record that justifies it (174290, extra firm/nigari, 9.98 g/100 g) is cited two sections later and never in the row. Compounding this, the claim that carries the whole section, "Branded records at FoodData Central put extra firm tofu from Nasoya, Kroger, Whole Foods, Wegmans and Pulmuone between 9.41 and 10.9 grams per 100 grams," names five retailers and a precise numeric band with zero links. I independently confirmed Nasoya at 10.1 g/100 g (8.0 g protein per 79 g serving), so the claim appears sound, but the page hands the reader nothing to check. That matters because this is precisely where the current top result (pinchofwellness.com) is wrong, presenting 17 g/100 g as "tofu" with no coagulant caveat, so the correction is this page's main competitive advantage and it is the one part a skeptical reader or an AI assistant cannot verify from the page itself.

Cook time never scales with fillet thickness. The recipe steps, the frontmatter cookTime, and the quickAnswer all hand the reader one flat window (10 to 12 minutes for the fish), and the quickAnswer is what an AI assistant will lift verbatim. Real supermarket fillets run roughly 0.5 inch at the tail to 1.5 inches at a center cut, a 2x to 3x spread in cook time. The body gestures at the problem ("start checking after eight minutes", "fold the narrow end underneath", "pull thin fillets as soon as they are ready") but never converts it into numbers, so a reader with a thick center cut who follows the flat 10 to 12 minutes and does not own a thermometer lands under 145 F on a page whose entire safety argument rests on 145 F. The competitor I checked (themediterraneandish.com) does give thickness-tiered timing, so this is a gap against the current top result, not just an abstract nitpick. Secondary, smaller gaps: salt and pepper are "to taste" with no gram or teaspoon anchor, which hurts reproducibility, and the vitamin D sentence applies raw-basis USDA values to a cooked fillet without saying so.

tests/high-fiber-fast-food-guide.test.mjs asserted a verified falsehood (that Panera PDF 403s automated requests). Test corrected to the measured truth: default curl UA returns HTTP 200 and a 513,680-byte PDF; a Chrome UA is what gets 403.

recovery.headline: Both channels recovered. Two separate technical causes, both found and fixed.

google.cause: functions/[[path]].js served noindex on canonical article URLs from 2026-05-18. Impressions fell 210/day to 2/day in 48 hours and stayed there for ~10 weeks. No Google penalty: manual actions and security issues both clean, confirmed by the owner.
google.fix_verified: All sitemap URLs return 200 with index,follow to a Googlebot user agent. seo_regression_check.py --live passes 9/9.
google.clicks: First clicks since the collapse: 2026-08-06 (1), 2026-08-09 (2, on bran-muffins and easy-sourdough-discard).
google.accelerant: 50 URL-inspection index requests submitted by the owner across 2026-08-01..08-12. Requested pages returned at positions 2 to 15; an untouched, unrequested control page sat at 55 to 64.

bing_ai_citations.cause: CC BY licence metadata stripped from datapackage.json on 2026-07-26 20:21. Citations fell 46 to 3 the next day and averaged ~5/day for 10 days.
bing_ai_citations.why_the_first_restore_failed: The licence was restored on 2026-07-29 at the PACKAGE level only. An AI consumer fetches a single CSV or one dataset object and never reads the wrapper, so it still saw no licence.
bing_ai_citations.fix: Declared per resource on 2026-08-05: datapackage.json 1 -> 25 declarations, and every dataset object in api-index-v1.json.
bing_ai_citations.verdict: Fully recovered. Pre-collapse typical range was 20-47/day with a peak of 51. Four sustained days at 23-45 confirm it. Clean natural experiment: the prediction was made in advance and a893205 was the only commit deployed in the window.
